name: Robert Wyatt
label: Rough Trade
lede: Robert Wyatt drummed and sang in the Soft Machine, fell from a fourth-floor window in 1973, and made his comeback on Rough Trade with a run of cover singles that ended in "Shipbuilding".

hero.by: Robert Wyatt in Louth, July 2013. Wikimedia Commons

eras.title: The lodger was Daevid Allen
eras.text: Wyatt grew up in a bohemian Kent household where an Australian beatnik rented a room and an American jazz drummer taught lessons. The Canterbury circle that formed around them gave him two bands and a way of singing nobody else had.

years.h: Born in Bristol to a BBC journalist
years.p: His mother, Honor Wyatt, works for the BBC; his father, George Ellidge, is an industrial psychologist. Actor Julian Glover is a half-brother.
years.xp: "It seemed perfectly normal to me," Wyatt said of an upbringing others called unconventional. His father joined the family when Robert was six and died ten years later, having retired early with multiple sclerosis: "so I was brought up a lot by women."

years.h: Drum lessons from George Neidorf, then Mallorca
years.p: At the family home in Lydden, near Dover, the American jazz drummer teaches him and Daevid Allen rents a room. In 1962 Wyatt and Neidorf move to Mallorca, near the poet Robert Graves.

years.h: The Daevid Allen Trio becomes the Wilde Flowers
years.p: Back in England he plays with Allen and Hugh Hopper. When Allen leaves for France, Wyatt and Hopper form The Wilde Flowers with Kevin Ayers and Richard Sinclair, and the drummer ends up singing lead.

years.cap: Kevin Ayers, Wyatt and Mike Ratledge in Dulwich Park
years.h: The Wilde Flowers split into Caravan and the Soft Machine
years.p: Ayers and Allen invite Wyatt and Mike Ratledge into Soft Machine. Wyatt drums and shares lead vocals, a combination a stage rock band almost never tried.

years.cap: Poster for the Hendrix and Soft Machine tour, 1968
yt: Soft Machine on French TV, August 1968
years.h: On tour with Hendrix, drinking with Keith Moon
years.p: Supporting the [[Jimi Hendrix|06fb1c8b-566e-4cb2-985b-b467c90781d4]] Experience across America, Wyatt, who hadn't drunk before, starts drinking hard. Keith Moon teaches him to alternate tequila and Southern Comfort.
years.xp: In a 2012 BBC Radio 4 profile Wyatt said he was an alcoholic by the early 1970s, and that without the accident that came next, the drinking and the recklessness would probably have killed him.

years.h: The End of an Ear, a solo album with tape effects
years.p: After chaotic touring, three Soft Machine albums and rising friction, Wyatt makes a record of his own voice, keyboards and tape manipulation.

eras.title: Machine molle, then a window in Maida Vale
eras.text: Pushed out of the Soft Machine's direction, Wyatt named his next band after it in French and was writing a second album when a party ended his life as a drummer.

years.cap: Soft Machine on the bill at the Deutschlandhalle, Berlin, March 1971
years.h: Wyatt quits the Soft Machine and starts Matching Mole
years.p: Unhappy at seeing his ideas rejected, he leaves. Matching Mole is a pun on machine molle, French for soft machine, and records two largely instrumental albums.

years.big: His own verdict, decades on: the fall probably saved his life.
years.src: Wikipedia: Robert Wyatt · The Guardian: I've no idea what's next
years.h: A fall from a fourth-floor window breaks Wyatt's spine
years.p: Drunk at a Maida Vale birthday party for Gong's Gilli Smyth and Lady June, Wyatt falls and is paralysed from the waist down. He has used a wheelchair ever since.
years.xp:
Friends of his partner Alfreda Benge stepped in: Jean Shrimpton gave them a car, and Julie Christie let them use a London flat, which they later bought from her.

Matching Mole was over. Wyatt kept playing percussion, jazz style, without his feet.

years.h: Pink Floyd play two shows in one day for Wyatt
years.p: [[Pink Floyd|83d91898-7763-47d7-b03b-b92132375c47]] headline the Rainbow Theatre twice, with the Soft Machine supporting and [[John Peel|e4dec348-ad10-43b6-a2b1-c22aab890675]] compering. The concerts raise a reported £10,000.

eras.title: Rock Bottom and the wicker chair
eras.text: With Pink Floyd's drummer producing, Wyatt finished the songs he'd started before the fall and had an unlikely hit. Virgin, his label, was less sure what to do with him.

years.h: Rock Bottom, written before the fall and finished after it
years.p: Nick Mason produces; Mike Oldfield, Ivor Cutler and [[Henry Cow|6ba2f6ce-50be-47df-b5a3-298ef032f476]]'s Fred Frith play. Wyatt rethinks the arrangements around his new circumstances during his convalescence.

yt: I'm a Believer, Top of the Pops, 1974
years.h: Top of the Pops wants him in a wicker chair
years.p: Wyatt's cover of the Monkees' "I'm a Believer" reaches No. 29. The show's producer says a wheelchair isn't suitable for family viewing; Wyatt wins.
years.xp: In one telling, Wyatt "lost his rag but not the wheelchair". The NME answered with a cover of the whole band in wheelchairs, a stand-in filling Mason's.

years.cap: Advert for the Drury Lane concert, September 1974
years.h: Back on stage at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane
years.p: A one-off concert, later released as Theatre Royal Drury Lane 8th September 1974.

years.cap: Advert for Ruth Is Stranger Than Richard, 1975
years.h: Brian Eno credited with "direct inject anti-jazz ray gun"
years.p: Ruth Is Stranger Than Richard leans into jazz and free jazz. Wyatt produces it himself, bar one Mason track.
years.xp: Before it, the follow-up single, a reggae remake of Chris Andrews' "Yesterday Man", got a low-key release; the boss at Virgin called it "lugubrious", and the delay sank its chances.

eras.title: Geoff Travis and the red singles
eras.text: Wyatt joined the Communist Party, and Rough Trade's Geoff Travis got him singing again. Because Virgin objected to him recording elsewhere, the comeback came as a run of cover singles: Chic, Violeta Parra, a 1940s gospel song about Stalin, and an anti-war ballad by Elvis Costello.

years.src: The Guardian: I've no idea what's next · Wikipedia: Robert Wyatt
years.h: Wyatt joins the Communist Party of Great Britain
years.p: He told the Guardian what drew him: it was internationalist and opposed to a totalitarian global empire.

years.src: The Guardian: Kevin Ayers and Robert Wyatt · The Guardian: I've no idea what's next
years.h: Geoff Travis coaxes him back to the microphone
years.p: With Virgin objecting, [[Rough Trade|4f4b0013-1704-4936-a769-e6e8a6e08ff8]] puts out singles of other people's songs, starting with Violeta Parra's "Arauco" and Chic's "At Last I Am Free".
years.xp:
The Guardian's Tim Cumming wrote that [[Geoff Travis|70437714-3183-4916-947f-e5ba2154d16a]] got Wyatt out of a Virgin deal that had left him with large debts and small royalties.

Simon Reynolds, also in the Guardian, put the Communist Party membership down to Wyatt's xenophilia, his instinctive sympathy for foreign cultures.

years.h: "Stalin Wasn't Stallin'" with a poem about Stalingrad
years.p: Wyatt covers the Golden Gate Jubilee Quartet's wartime song and puts Peter Blackman reading his poem "Stalingrad" on the B-side.

years.h: Keyboards on Scritti Politti's "The 'Sweetest Girl'"
years.p: Wyatt plays on Green Gartside's turn toward pop for [[Scritti Politti|a2588b38-6532-4186-b0c8-9aff306d56f5]], his Rough Trade labelmates.

years.h: Nothing Can Stop Us, one Wyatt song and ten others
years.p: The singles collection runs from Chic to Billie Holiday's "Strange Fruit" and "The Red Flag". The sleeve is by Alfreda Benge.

q: All I thought about was singing it in tune!
years.h: Travis posts Wyatt a cassette of "Shipbuilding"
years.p: Clive Langer wrote the tune with Wyatt in mind; Elvis Costello wrote the words about the Falklands War. Wyatt cuts his vocal in a couple of hours with Costello producing.
years.xp:
Costello had already recorded a vocal, and the plan was to release that. Mark Bedford of [[Madness|5f58803e-8c4c-478e-8b51-477f38483ede]] played double bass, Steve Nieve piano.

Five picture sleeves used sections of Stanley Spencer's 1940s panels Shipbuilding on the Clyde. The single didn't chart that summer.

years.h: Reissued, "Shipbuilding" gives Rough Trade its first Top 40
years.p: Re-released a year after the war, it reaches No. 35. NME writers had already voted it their third favourite song of 1982.

years.h: Old Rottenhat, his first album of his own songs in ten years
years.p: Strongly political and sparse, played mostly by Wyatt alone.

years.h: Tears for Fears write "I Believe" for him
years.p: Roland Orzabal dedicates the Songs from the Big Chair track to Wyatt and covers "Sea Song" on the B-side.

eras.title: A sabbatical in Spain
eras.text: After guest spots with Ryuichi Sakamoto and others, Wyatt and Benge went to Spain for a while. He came back with an album built at home.

years.h: Dondestan, the comeback after Spain
years.p: Wyatt and Benge return from their sabbatical with the album. Years later it became the record people played to clear a pub.

years.h: Shleep draws more praise
years.p: Released on Hannibal, it's one of his best-received records.

eras.title: Meltdown, Björk and Domino
eras.text: Into his late fifties Wyatt became a guest everyone wanted, from David Gilmour to Björk to Hot Chip, and a curator in his own right.

years.h: Wyatt curates Meltdown and sings "Comfortably Numb" with Gilmour
years.p: At the South Bank festival he joins David Gilmour on the Pink Floyd song, captured on Gilmour's concert DVD.

years.src: The Guardian: I've no idea what's next · Wikipedia: Robert Wyatt
years.h: Cuckooland gets a Mercury nomination
years.p: Gilmour, Paul Weller and Brian Eno guest. Wyatt has taken up the trumpet as well.
years.xp: "I didn't want to feel pinned down as a singer, and the trumpet frees me from that," he told the Guardian. He and Benge were then working from artist studios on Bermondsey Street in south London.

years.h: Björk brings him in for "Submarine"
years.p: Wyatt sings on the Medúlla track, the album [[Björk|87c5dedd-371d-4a53-9f7f-80522fb7f3cb]] built almost entirely from voices.

q: I'm very honoured at the idea of becoming a verb.
years.h: "Wyatting": playing Dondestan on pub jukeboxes
years.p: Bloggers coin a verb for clearing a pub with Wyatt songs. He finds it funny; Benge says she'd like to punch the man who coined it.
years.xp: Wyatt, to the Guardian: "I think it's really funny." Benge's objection was that it used him to let clever people feel superior, "so unlike Robert, because he's so appreciative of the strengths of pop music."

years.src: The Guardian: Kevin Ayers and Robert Wyatt · Wikipedia: Robert Wyatt
years.h: Comicopera, in three acts, on Domino
years.p: Benge writes many of the lyrics. Domino reissues his back catalogue the following year.

eras.title: Fifty years in the saddle
eras.text: Wyatt told Uncut he'd stopped, a better word than retired, he said. The work kept travelling without him, into a biography, a Radio 4 Book of the Week and an animated film.

years.big: "Fifty years in the saddle, it's not nothing."
years.src: Uncut: Robert Wyatt: I've stopped making music · Wikipedia: Robert Wyatt
years.h: Wyatt tells Uncut he's stopped making music
years.p: He cites age and a bigger appetite for politics. Marcus O'Dair's authorised biography, Different Every Time, comes out the same month.
years.xp: "I thought, train drivers retire when they're 65, so I will, as well," he told Uncut. "There is a pride in [stopping], I don't want it to go off."

years.h: One last stage, at a concert for Jeremy Corbyn
years.p: Wyatt appears at the Brighton Dome with Paul Weller and Danny Thompson for the Labour leader, his most recent public appearance.

years.cap: Stencil mural of Wyatt in Canterbury, 2024
years.h: Rock Bottom becomes an animated film
years.p: María Trénor's feature, built on Wyatt's life and music, plays in competition at Annecy.
